title: The Mool Mantar at the summit
word: The Mool Mantar at the summit
hook: the words from day four, now understood
tomorrow: the Japji's first seven pauris, read whole. what holds them together?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lived year close: a year of gurpurabs, lived, not just learned. Now the last climb of the path begins, and it begins where the Granth does.

A song you knew as a kid can hit differently years later. Same words, same tune, and one line you used to sing without thinking suddenly sounds like it's about you. The Mool Mantar works like that. It was among the first words on this path, at the top of the Granth's first page. The words haven't moved. So, at the start of the summit: do they sound the same now?
screen: `A CHILDHOOD SONG, HEARD AGAIN.` → `THE FIRST WORDS ON THE PATH.` → `DO THEY SOUND THE SAME?`

segments.voice: Say it slowly and listen to how it's built. Ik oankaar: One, written as a numeral, joined to the sound Oankar. Sat naam: truth is the name. Kartaa purakh: the creator, the being who makes. Nirbhau, nirvair: without fear, without hate. Akaal moorat: a form beyond time. Ajoonee, saibhan: unborn, self-existent. Gur prasaad: known by the Guru's grace. Macauliffe's translation opens it this way: "There is but one God whose name is true, the Creator." Now listen to the sound. The middle runs on short, firm words, nirbhau, nirvair, almost like footsteps. The end softens: gur prasaad, by grace, an open hand after all that description. A year lived has filled those words in. Nirbhau, without fear: Guru Tegh Bahadur walking to Delhi himself. Nirvair, without hate: a Nawab from another faith speaking up for two boys. Kartaa purakh: a harvest at Vaisakhi. And gur prasaad: a lamp lit at the door for someone coming home. Nothing new is added at the summit. The first words, said slowly enough to hear what they've been holding all along.
screen: `ONE, TRUTH, CREATOR.` · `FEARLESS, WITHOUT HATE, TIMELESS.` · `IT ENDS ON GRACE.` · `A YEAR LIVED FILLS THEM IN.` · then, large: `THE SAME WORDS, DEEPER.`

segments.voice: Say the Mool Mantar out loud, as slowly as you can, one phrase for each breath: ik oankaar, sat naam, kartaa purakh, nirbhau, nirvair, akaal moorat, ajoonee, saibhan, gur prasaad. If the Gurmukhi is new to you, say the English instead: One, truth, creator, without fear, without hate, timeless, unborn, self-existent, grace. Then go round once more, slower.
The Mool Mantar at the summit. The Granth's opening words, said again at the top of the path, and heard with a year behind them.
screen: `THE MOOL MANTAR AT THE SUMMIT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Carry this: the same words, deeper, because the one saying them has changed. Day one of the summit.

screen: `DAY 1761 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 1 OF 31.` → `TOMORROW: THE JAPJI'S FIRST SEVEN PAURIS, READ WHOLE. WHAT HOLDS THEM TOGETHER?`

howItsDone: The Mool Mantar opens the Guru Granth Sahib and the Japji; Sikhs recite it in the morning prayers, and families often teach it to children first, sometimes saying it slowly together, phrase by phrase.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape senses. Sound carries the idea: the Mool Mantar said slowly, firm in the middle, soft at the end; the practice is saying it aloud phrase by phrase. First day of Block D (the summit, 1 of 31). Answers day 1760's question; tomorrow's question (what holds Japji pauris 1-7 together) is answered by day 1762's hook.

The index hook says 'the words from day four'; on this path the Mool Mantar is taught on days 10-11 (camp one) and day 159, and day 4 is the Panj Pyare. The script avoids the day number ('among the first words on this path'). Suggest correcting the outline line.
Macauliffe quotation reused exactly as vetted on day 10. The transliteration follows the common romanization; confirm.
Links to the past year (Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Nawab of Malerkotla, Vaisakhi, Bandi Chhor lamps) are offered as illustrations of the words, not as the Granth's own glosses.
Storyline: Bebe (the weekly elder) has Simran say the Mool Mantar with her slowly, the way she taught her as a child; Simran is weeks from leaving for college.
